item.title: Phenotype-structured nonlocal aggregation models I: signal production and response
item.description: arXiv:2610.29884v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Individuals within a cellular or ecological population can exhibit substantial variation in their traits or phenotype. Such heterogeneity can fundamentally alter population-level behaviour, including the ability to aggregate and form spatial patterns. We investigate these effects by extending nonlocal aggregation models, widely used to model cell--cell adhesion and collective animal movement, to incorporate phenotype structure. We characterise how heterogeneity and switching between phenotypes affect whether patterns form, how phenotypes are distributed within them, and whether they are stationary or exhibit spatio-temporal oscillations. We show that pattern formation is promoted when phenotypes that produce stronger interaction signals also respond more strongly to them, whereas specialisation towards either signal production or response inhibits pattern formation. Increasing rates of switching between phenotypes dampen these effects. Heterogeneity can also enable weakly interacting, and even repulsive, individuals to pattern as part of the collective. Furthermore, movement in phenotype and physical space can interact to restructure patterns and generate spatio-temporal oscillations. A further key message of this study is the value of considering both discrete $N$-phenotype and continuous phenotype formulations. We develop both in parallel, demonstrating formal correspondences, but also advantages to each framework in terms of mathematical analyses and interpretability.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Jun Jewell, Andrew L. Krause, Philip K. Maini, Eamonn A. Gaffney

item.title: Quantifying reticulocyte biomechanics in health and disease
item.description: arXiv:2607.21810v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) populations are mechanically and morphologically heterogeneous, yet how this heterogeneity governs transport, splenic retention and blood rheology in confinement remains unclear. We combine microchannel experiments with dissipative particle dynamics (DPD) simulations to determine how the morphology, deformability and hydrodynamic interaction of immature RBCs (reticulocytes) shape microconfined flow in acute and chronic mountain sickness. Reticulocyte-rich samples present the three shapes that the maturation literature assigns to successive reticulocyte stages -- multilobular, cup-shaped and near-discocytic -- which we model as R1-R3, each with a membrane shear modulus within the range reported for reticulocytes. A 5-um microchannel resolves these models only weakly, R1 taking at most ~18% longer than control discocytes to cross it, whereas a 1.5-um splenic slit, driven at its own loading, delays R1 by ~30%; both geometries order the models by shear modulus. In cell pairs, a leading cell never lets a follower pass below its own single-cell threshold, ruling out the order-of-magnitude reduction that a wake-"unjamming" picture would suggest; instead the follower queues behind the leader, and a stiffer leader, which clears the slit more slowly, delays it more. The controlling variable is the single-cell critical pressure gradient Delta P_c, which rises monotonically from control discocytes through the reticulocyte subtypes to sickled cells. Set against published rheograms, an analytical estimate attributes chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity mainly to hematocrit-driven crowding rather than single-cell rheology. These results place benign acclimatization, chronic-mountain-sickness hyperviscosity and sickle-cell-trait splenic syndrome on a single mechanical axis defined by Delta P_c.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis

item.title: Optimal concentration and gradient sensing by perfect monitors
item.description: arXiv:2608.08816v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cells often estimate chemical concentrations from only a few diffusing molecules, whose stochastic motion limits sensing precision. We consider a perfect monitoring instrument that records the instantaneous molecular density throughout a finite region without perturbing the concentration field or distinguishing molecular identities. The standard Berg-Purcell estimator weights all positions uniformly. Here we derive the optimal spatial weighting within a large class of unbiased estimators for both concentration and gradient sensing. Variance minimization maps to an electrostatic problem. Surprisingly, although the instrument monitors the entire volume, the optimal estimator assigns all weight to its boundary, reducing the uncertainty in both concentration and gradient sensing. We extend the results to arbitrary geometries and spatial dimensions.
item.dc:creator: Farshid Jafarpour

item.title: The typical red cell makes too little vacuole material for coalescence to build the large vacuoles of pocked cells
item.description: arXiv:2610.22646v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Red blood cells carrying intracellular vacuoles, called pocked cells, are a sensitive marker of splenic function: about 0.5% of cells in healthy people, 20 to 70% after splenectomy. Vacuoles too small to see are common, and visible ones are thought to grow when small ones merge. We tested that idea with a particle model that resolves the cell's membrane, its contents and every vacuole, and with an inventory of the vacuole volume a cell can make. In tube, shear and vascular flows, a cell's vacuoles met within a second, and, allowed to fuse, ten merged into one to five. Meeting is not what limits growth; material is. At the rate measured after splenectomy, all the vacuoles an average cell makes in its 120-day life fuse into one body 0.6 $\mu$m across, the size healthy cells carry, but 16 times smaller in volume than the 1.5-$\mu$m bodies of patients without a spleen. Taking vacuole size as set at formation, a population model in which vacuoles are made mainly in young cells, and far faster in a small minority that alone makes material for a large one, accounts for the published counts, sizes and age profiles and, on first-hand measurements, favours a splenic clearance that rises several-fold as cells age; letting that minority's vacuoles fuse fits nearly as well. At a model splenic slit, the cell's spare surface decided passage, and a vacuole mattered only when it led. A slit experiment would test whether brief encounters fuse vacuoles.
item.dc:creator: Zhaojie Chai, Jianlu Zheng, He Li, Ming Dao, George Em Karniadakis
